Streams in the Data Flow

Three arrows in; the third, Streams, is today

Batch Processing

Batch: collect, then process, then deliver. Delay: minutes to days

Stream Processing

Streaming: each record flows as it happens. Almost real-time

The shift to event-driven systems has already begun…
From a static snapshot…

This leads us to …

Kafka carries events into batch, near-real-time, and live processing paths

Kafka

Everything that emits events on top, everything that wants them below, one log in between

Kafka – Producers

Producers write and get an acknowledgement; they never know the readers

Kafka – Brokers

Brokers store events on local disk for a retention time: a store, not a queue

Kafka – Consumers

Consumers poll, forever, at their own pace

Decoupling Producers and Consumers

  • Producers and Consumers are decoupled
  • Slow Consumers do not affect Producers
  • Add Consumers without affecting Producers
  • Failure of Consumer does not affect System
The log in the middle lets each side fail, slow down or grow alone

Case study: Kafka at LinkedInLinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 to distribute activity and operational events

With all-to-all integration, a shared log reduces endpoint connections from n×m to n+m

Data Elements

Metadata and optional headers on top; key and value, both bytes, as the body

Topics

  • Topics: streams of “related” messages in Kafka
    • Is a logical representation
    • Categorizes messages into groups
  • Developers define topics
  • Producer ↔ topic: N to N relation
  • Unlimited number of topics
A topic is a named stream: the nearest thing to a table

Topic, Partition, Segment

Topic → partitions (each a log) → segments (rolling files on disk)

An Append-Only Log

It's a log: an ordered, persistent sequence of events, append-only

Order Within a Partition

Topics are split into partitions: order holds within one partition, not across

Writing to Partitions

Producers write to topic partitions, at the end

Reading Without Deleting

Consumers read from topic partitions; reading removes nothing

Broker Replication: Fault Tolerance

Here each partition has a leader and two followers on different brokers

Producer

Serialize, pick a partition, compress, buffer, send a batch

Producer – Partitioning Strategy

  • Producers use a partitioning strategy to assign each message to a partition
  • Two purposes:
    • Load balancing
    • Semantic partitioning
  • Partitioning strategy specified by producer
    • With a key: hash(key) % number_of_partitions
    • No key → spread over partitions (sticky batches since Kafka 2.4)
  • Custom partitioner possible

Producer – Accumulate Messages

send() returns at once; records accumulate per partition in the buffer

Producer – Send Message Batches

Batches go to each partition’s leader; one request per broker

Consumer

• connect to broker(s) and cache metadata
• subscribe to topic(s)
• join consumer group
• continuously: poll records from broker(s) and commit offsets

Consumer – Offsets

An offset is a position in the log; each consumer keeps its own

Consumer – Groups

Within a group a partition has one reader; different groups each read everything

Consumer – Group Rebalancing

Partitions are reassigned as consumers come and go; partitions cap the parallelism

Demo: Partitions and Consumer GroupsFive machines send keyed events; change the group, then crash a consumer before it commits

Partitions 3Consumers 2
 

Answer: Partitions and Consumer GroupsExplain the key order, parallelism limit, and replay after a crash

ChangeObservationReason
Produce for M1Same partition; increasing offsetsKey mapping is fixed
3 partitions; 4 consumersOne consumer is idleOne owner per partition in this group
Crash before commit; poll againPreviously processed records repeatRestart from the committed offset
The stored log and the committed offset determine what is read

Caveat: At-Least-Once DuplicatesProcess, then crash before the commit: the restart reads the same records again

Remedy: deduplicate by event ID, recorded in the same transaction as the side effect
The commit never happened, so offsets 4 to 6 are processed twice

Conclusion: Scalable Data Pipeline

Add producers, brokers or consumers independently: that is the point

Programming in Kafka

How do I get streams of data into and out of Kafka?

Kafka Connect Sources and Sinks

Source connectors in, sink connectors out: configuration, not code

A Continuous ETL Flow

Extract (source connector), transform (Streams), load (sink connector)

Kafka Connect Workers

Connector tasks spread over workers; configs live in a Kafka topic

Change Data Capture

StepWhat happensTypical tool
1. A row changesan app runs INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on its databasePostgreSQL, MySQL
2. The change is readfrom the database log, not by re-querying the tableDebezium on Kafka Connect
3. It becomes an eventone message per change, in order, on a topicKafka
4. Others reactwarehouse, search index, cache stay in syncsink connectors, Flink
Read the database log and send every change as an event

Kafka Streams as a Library

A library, not a cluster: your app reads a topic, transforms, writes a topic

Continuous Transformations

filter, map, join, aggregate, on an unbounded stream

Confluent KSQL

Develop real-time stream processing apps writing only SQL!
No Java, Python, or other boilerplate to wrap around it.
CREATE STREAM vip_actions AS
  SELECT   userid, page, action
  FROM     clickstream c
  LEFT JOIN users u ON c.userid = u.user_id
  WHERE    u.level = 'Platinum';

Event Time vs Arrival TimeAn event can arrive after the time window in which it happened

EventHappened atArrived at10:00–10:05 window
P-17 overheats10:0410:04count it now
P-17 alarm10:0310:07late for this window
The alarm belongs to the earlier window by event time

Watermarks and Late EventsA later close improves completeness but keeps window state longer

At 10:07PolicyResult for the 10:00–10:05 window
Alarm from 10:03 arrivesclose immediately at 10:05miss the alarm
Alarm from 10:03 arriveswait for late events until 10:08revise the count
Latency and completeness move together when events arrive late

Example – Create Topic

Before you can write your first events, you must create a topic. Open another terminal session and run:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic quickstart-events --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
All of Kafka’s command line tools have additional options. Run kafka-topics.sh without arguments to display usage information, or describe the new topic:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic quickstart-events --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Topic: quickstart-events   TopicId: NPmZHyhbR9y00wWglMH2sg   PartitionCount: 1   ReplicationFactor: 1
  Topic: quickstart-events   Partition: 0   Leader: 0   Replicas: 0   Isr: 0

Example – Process Events with Kafka Streams

To give you a first taste, here’s how one would implement the popular WordCount algorithm:
KStream<String, String> textLines = builder.stream("quickstart-events");

KTable<String, Long> wordCounts = textLines
            .flatMapValues(line -> Arrays.asList(line.toLowerCase().split(" ")))
            .groupBy((keyIgnored, word) -> word)
            .count();

wordCounts.toStream().to("output-topic", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));
The same WordCount as Lecture 13’s MapReduce and Spark, now updated with every new line: a KTable is a count that never finishes.

Takeaway: Big Data III

1Kafka stores ongoing events in partitioned logs; order holds within a partition
2Consumer groups scale reading, but a crash before an offset commit can replay events
3Connect moves events; a stream processor computes by event time and must handle late arrivals
